summary: Specifies DHCPv6 options, called Softwire46 options, to configure Customer Edge devices that use address-plus-port schemes for IPv4 over IPv6. The options carry the parameters for those schemes.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines DHCPv6 options that give a customer router the settings it needs to provide IPv4 service across an IPv6-only network. The router requests a container for its chosen mechanism, and the server returns the matching settings inside it.

questions: how does a map-e ce get its configuration
subtitle: How DHCPv6 supplies a customer router with settings for IPv4 service over IPv6.

tldr.problem: A Customer Edge device using an IPv4-over-IPv6 service needs its IPv4 address or mapping rules, port allocation details, and information about the IPv6-side relay or prefix.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five common DHCPv6 options and three container options for MAP-E, MAP-T, and Lightweight 4over6. A client requests a container, and the server places the configuration options inside it.
tldr.outcome: The defined options give the three mechanisms a shared way to deliver their configuration. RFC 7598 is updated by RFC 8539.

today: RFC 7598 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8539. It defines DHCPv6 options for MAP-E, MAP-T, and Lightweight 4over6 configuration.

sections.title: Why Softwire46 Needs Configuration
sections.content:
Softwire46 refers to designs that provide IPv4 connectivity across an IPv6 network using an IPv4 address together with transport-layer ports. A Customer Edge (CE) router needs these service parameters before it can offer IPv4 connectivity to devices on its network.

This RFC defines DHCPv6 options for sending those parameters to a CE. It does not cover unrelated IPv4 settings or configuration of the Border Relay.
sections.plainLanguage: A router connecting an IPv4 network through an IPv6 service needs its service settings first. This RFC explains how a DHCPv6 server sends those settings to the router.

sections.title: Three IPv4-over-IPv6 Mechanisms
sections.content:
The option family configures MAP-E, MAP-T, and Lightweight 4over6. All provide IPv4 service to a CE across an IPv6-only access network, but they carry traffic differently: MAP-E tunnels IPv4 over IPv6, MAP-T translates between IPv4 and IPv6, and Lightweight 4over6 uses hub-and-spoke tunneling.

Each mechanism has a container option. A client asks for the container code in its DHCPv6 Option Request Option. Provisioning options outside a container MUST be silently ignored by the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC covers three ways to carry IPv4 service across an IPv6 network. The client asks for the container matching its mechanism, and the server puts that mechanism's settings inside it.

sections.title: The Common Configuration Options
sections.content:
The common options describe mapping rules, a Border Relay IPv6 address, a default mapping prefix, an IPv4-to-IPv6 address binding, and port-set parameters. MAP-E and MAP-T use rule options; Lightweight 4over6 uses the address-binding option.

A rule can be marked for forwarding with its F-flag. If that flag is not set, the rule is only a Basic Mapping Rule and MUST NOT be used for forwarding. Port parameters can identify the port set assigned to a CE when addresses are shared.
sections.plainLanguage: The common options carry the address, mapping, relay, and port details a device needs. The F-flag distinguishes a rule that can be used for forwarding from one that cannot.

sections.title: Port Sets for Shared Addresses
sections.content:
When several CEs share an IPv4 address, each may receive a different set of transport ports. The optional OPTION_S46_PORTPARAMS carries an offset, the number of significant PSID bits, and the Port Set Identifier (PSID).

If the PSID length is zero, the PSID field is ignored. When a client receives an explicit PSID, it MUST use that value when configuring its softwire interface. The option is carried inside a rule or address-binding option.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared IPv4 address can be divided into separate port sets for different customer routers. The port-parameters option tells a router which set to use.

sections.title: Containers and Their Required Contents
sections.content:
Each container groups the options for one mechanism and domain. MAP-E requires at least one rule and one Border Relay option. MAP-T requires at least one rule and exactly one Default Mapping Rule option. Lightweight 4over6 requires at least one Border Relay option and permits at most one address-binding option.

Some common options are optional or forbidden in each container. A client MUST silently ignore a container that violates the option requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Each mechanism has a different list of required and optional settings. A client discards a container that does not follow the list for its mechanism.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
By default, a DHCPv6 server does not send a Softwire46 container unless the client requests it. A client MUST request the containers for which it is configured in its specified DHCPv6 message types.

A client MUST support multiple rule options in MAP-E and MAP-T containers. If it receives an unsupported option or invalid value, it SHOULD discard that container and log the event. A CE configures each network interface separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The client must request the containers it can use. If a returned container has an unsupported option or invalid value, the client should discard it and record the problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like other DHCPv6 configuration, Softwire46 settings could be supplied by a third party in the middle. The RFC says that access through MAP or Lightweight 4over6 cannot therefore be trusted by itself, and firewalls or other security mechanisms should remain in place.

In an IPv6-only network without IPv4 firewalls, a device could be misled into enabling IPv4 and sending traffic to an attacker. The RFC points readers to the security guidance for the three underlying mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: A device cannot assume that Softwire46 settings are trustworthy just because they arrived through DHCPv6. Keep other security controls, such as IP firewalls, in place.
